title: Forgetting what's behind (Philippians 3:13–14)

lines: A PAST TO BE PROUD OF.
A PAST TO BE HAUNTED BY.
cards: Paul had two pasts, and either one could have held him in place. The first was a past to be proud of.
In Philippians he lists it: circumcised on the eighth day, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews, a Pharisee, blameless in keeping the law. The second was a past to be haunted by.
He'd persecuted the church, dragging believers off to prison. One past could make him proud. The other could make him despair.
Today he says what he does with both.

teach.b: He's just said he counts all his gains as loss for the sake of knowing Christ.

Then: "Brethren, I do not count myself to have apprehended. But one thing I do: forgetting the things that are behind, and stretching forth myself to those that are before, I press towards the mark, to the prize of the supernal vocation of God in Christ Jesus."

Stretching forth is one Greek word, epekteinomenos, straining forward, like a runner leaning toward the finish. The mark is the finish post a runner fixes his eyes on. The prize is the wreath at the end.
Supernal vocation means the upward call: God calling from above. Now notice what forgetting can't mean here. Paul hasn't lost his memory.
He's just listed his whole past in detail.

teach.h: FORGETTING: THE PAST NO LONGER STEERS.
teach.b: Forgetting means the past no longer steers. A runner knows the track behind him is there. He just doesn't run looking at it.
And Paul says plainly he hasn't arrived. He's still running. Saint Gregory of Nyssa built a whole picture of the spiritual life on this one word.
He said the soul never stops stretching toward God, because God never runs out. Catholics put this into practice in confession.
The Church teaches that sins confessed and absolved are truly forgiven, and a confessor may tell someone who keeps re-confessing old sins, out of worry, to stop: it's already behind you.
The pride and the shame both get left on the track. One thing I do, Paul says. Just one.

how: Catholics confess their sins in the sacrament of penance and believe absolved sins are truly forgiven; confessors counsel people troubled by scruples not to re-confess sins already forgiven.

o: wiping every memory of your past for good
pretending your old mistakes never happened
letting the past stop steering while you run on

games.q: the runner's sentence — tap the pairs.
p: the soul always stretching toward God

s: 'forgetting' means Paul had erased his past
he's just listed it in detail; the past simply no longer steers.
Paul says he has already arrived
"I do not count myself to have apprehended."
he lists it among the things behind him.

games.q: you're Paul, with a proud record and a shameful one. what do you do with them?
o: build on the proud one and hide the other.
keep confessing the shameful one forever.
forget what's behind and press towards the mark.
games.why: "forgetting the things that are behind, and stretching forth myself to those that are before, I press towards the mark."

practice: Think of one old failure you still replay: something you said, a year you wasted, a way you hurt someone.
If you've made it right, confessed it, or done what you could, picture it on the track behind you, then turn and face forward, toward one step today.
If you pray, hand the old failure to God and ask for the next step; if not, simply notice which way you're facing.

wordCard.voice: Forgetting what's behind. Paul's runner's sentence: forgetting the past, stretching toward what's ahead, pressing toward the mark. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a mark to aim at, the goal a runner fixes his eyes on (Philippians 3:14).

carryVoice: Your line: press on. And that's week eighty-four: baros, by grace, breadth, one Lord, panoplia, kenosis, and forgetting what's behind. That's day five hundred eighty-eight.

sources.ref: Gregory of Nyssa, The Life of Moses
